The question of whether ancient Egyptians had electricity is a topic where mainstream scholarly opinion and fringe/pseudohistorical claims sharply diverge. According to a USA TODAY fact-check citing Egyptologists, including a UC Berkeley professor, "Ancient Egyptians did not have modern electricity," and the Temple of Hathor carvings often cited as evidence "simply show religious symbols, not proof of electrical technology" [d1]. Wikipedia's article on Ancient Egyptian technology similarly notes that "no evidence of anything used to manipulate electricity had been found in Egypt" and that suggestions of Egyptian electrical knowledge stem from misreadings of ancient texts [d2]. The complete absence of archaeological evidence — no lightbulbs, no power plants, no electrical wiring — while oil lamps have been found in large quantities, further undermines the electricity claim [d5]; archaeologists and Egyptologists have also specifically dismissed the Dendera light bulb carving as depicting a creation myth, not electrical technology [d7].

On the other side, low-credibility sources claim ancient Egyptians had primitive solar power constructed from obsidian and copper wire, chemical batteries used for electroplating, and even pyramid-based power plants [d3, d4, d6]. These claims, attributed to an unverified "International Journal of Antiquity" and unsupported by mainstream scholarship, represent the fringe pseudohistorical perspective. Ancient Egyptians were aware of natural electrical phenomena such as lightning and electric fish — referred to as "Thunderers of the Nile" — but awareness of natural phenomena is distinct from possessing electrical technology [d8].
